nameStory: The tiny bluet gets its name from its diminutive stature - at just 6 inches tall or less, it's the smallest member of the bluet family you'll find in New England. The word 'bluet' comes from the French word for blue, referring to the delicate blue-toned petals that make these flowers so charming despite their small size.
description: Tiny bluet is a petite wildflower that forms low rosettes of small leaves close to the ground. This little plant rarely grows taller than 6 inches and produces dainty four-petaled flowers that are pale blue to white with sunny yellow centers. Each flower is only about a quarter-inch across, but what they lack in size they make up for in delicate beauty. The plant spreads by self-seeding to form small colonies in sunny, rocky areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny four-petaled flowers about 1/4 inch across with pale blue to white petals and bright yellow centers - they feel papery-thin to the touch and have no noticeable scent

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a low rosette of leaves at ground level, rarely exceeding 6 inches in height, with individual flower stems arising from leaf joints

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small oval leaves up to half an inch long arranged in opposite pairs, feeling smooth and slightly succulent with a fresh green color

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Each flower sits alone at the end of a thin stem that emerges from where leaves meet the main stem (leaf axils)

habitat: Look for tiny bluet in sunny, well-drained spots with thin soil, especially on rocky ledges, granite outcrops, and dry open areas where grass is sparse. It thrives in slightly acidic soil and needs full sun exposure. In New England, you're most likely to spot it on exposed rock faces, along rocky trails, or in thin-soiled meadows.

seasonality.spring: Flowers begin blooming in late spring, creating tiny dots of blue and white against the rocky ground. The small rosettes of fresh green leaves are most noticeable now.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming continues into early summer, with the brightest and most numerous flowers appearing during this time.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin setting seed and the flowers fade, leaving behind small seed capsules. Basal leaves may persist but become less conspicuous.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back to ground level, with seeds waiting in the soil to germinate the following spring.

funFact: Despite being one of our tiniest wildflowers, tiny bluet is a close relative of coffee plants - they're both members of the madder family, which includes over 13,000 species worldwide ranging from tiny ground-huggers to tropical trees!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with its larger cousin, azure bluet, but tiny bluet stays much closer to the ground and has smaller flowers. Remember: tiny bluet forms tight rosettes and rarely gets above ankle height, while azure bluet grows more upright and can reach a foot tall.
contextualKnowledge: Tiny bluet is quite rare in New England, with only 19 recorded observations in the region - it's much more common in the southeastern United States. Finding one here is a special treat, as you're seeing a plant at the very northern edge of its range.
compareHints: Tiny bluet is much smaller than azure bluet, which grows taller and has larger flowers, and more compact than long-leaved bluets, which have narrow elongated leaves. Summer bluet has purplish flowers rather than blue ones. The rosette growth form and extremely small stature make tiny bluet distinctive among New England bluets.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Azure bluet is much smaller than its cousin long-leaved bluets, which can grow up to a foot tall with narrow, lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's bluets, long-leaved bluet stands out for its narrow leaves and preference for dry, sandy soils.
Among New England's bluets, summer bluet is the woodland lover while azure bluet prefers sunny meadows.
